body:
Sorry for the big patch.  Think of this PR as "object shapes" but for ActiveRecord objects.

I want to change the storage strategy of ActiveRecord objects to use an array under the hood.  It's much easier to optimize array access than it is to optimize hash access, and I think in many cases we can see a reduction in memory as well (a "right sized" array should take less memory than a hash storing the same number of elements).

With this PR, fast path readers will look up attributes by index rather than by name.  The index (or "slot") is calculated from the database schema.

For example, if we have a `Post` model with a table like this:

| column      | SQL type  | slot | cast type |
|-------------|-----------|-----:|-----------|
| `id`        | `integer` |    0 | `Integer` |
| `title`     | `varchar` |    1 | `String`  |
| `score`     | `integer` |    2 | `Integer` |
| `published` | `boolean` |    3 | `Boolean` |

Reader methods are generated per slot rather than per attribute name.  Each slot gets one method, defined once in a module that's shared by every model:

```ruby
def slot_0
  _read_attribute_at!(0)
end

def slot_1
  _read_attribute_at!(1)
end

def slot_2
  _read_attribute_at!(2)
end

def slot_3
  _read_attribute_at!(3)
end
```

Then each model defines its readers from those methods, under the attribute's name:

```ruby
class Post < ActiveRecord::Base
  # Done by define_attribute_methods
  define_method(:id,        SlotMethods.instance_method(:slot_0))
  define_method(:title,     SlotMethods.instance_method(:slot_1))
  define_method(:score,     SlotMethods.instance_method(:slot_2))
  define_method(:published, SlotMethods.instance_method(:slot_3))
end
```

So `Post#title` behaves as if it were `def title = _read_attribute_at!(1)`.  Since the method body only depends on the slot, every model with a column in slot 1 shares the same method (and the same iseq), so the number of reader methods grows with the width of the widest table rather than with the total number of columns across all models.  For comparison, `main` generates one method per attribute name that calls `_read_attribute!("title")`.

`_read_attribute_at!` reads the value straight out of the attribute set by index, and only deals with missing attributes when the fast path raises:

```ruby
def _read_attribute_at!(index)
  @attributes.fetch_value_at!(index)
rescue ActiveModel::MissingAttributeError
  attr_name = @attributes.name_at(index)
  raise if @attributes.key?(attr_name)
  missing_attribute(attr_name, caller_locations)
end
```

The upside is that we can read attributes very fast (only array lookups, no hash lookups).  The down side is that since the array index is burned in to the code, we're forced to always have a backing array that is at least as wide as the table.  In other words, we're optimizing for selecting all columns.

For this benchmark:

```ruby
# Usage: ruby [--yjit|--zjit] read_all.rb RAILS_ROOT
%w[activesupport activemodel activerecord].each { |l| $LOAD_PATH.unshift "#{ARGV[0]}/#{l}/lib" }
require "active_record"
require "benchmark/ips"

ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(adapter: "sqlite3", database: ":memory:")
ActiveRecord::Migration.verbose = false
ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :posts do |t|
    t.string :title
    t.integer :score
    t.boolean :published
  end
end

class Post < ActiveRecord::Base; end
Post.insert_all(1000.times.map { |i| { title: "Post #{i}", score: i, published: i.even? } })

Benchmark.ips do |x|
  x.report("load 1000 + read all") do
    Post.all.each { |p| p.id; p.title; p.score; p.published }
  end
end
```

We get this result (`ruby 4.1.0dev (2026-10-14 master b709bdb3e3) [arm64-darwin25]`, `main` is the merge base `1d11045254`):

|             |      main |    branch | speedup   |
|-------------|----------:|----------:|:----------|
| Interpreter | 312.3 i/s | 364.7 i/s | **1.17x** |
| YJIT        | 840.8 i/s | 1,068 i/s | **1.27x** |
| ZJIT        | 1,015 i/s | 1,320 i/s | **1.30x** |


## Internal layout details

If the `Post` model in this example had an extra `attribute :blah`, and we also selected extra data, the array layout would be like this:

| slot | attribute | from | reader |
|:-:|---|---|---|
| 0 | `id` | column | `slot_0` |
| 1 | `title` | column | `slot_1` |
| 2 | `score` | column | `slot_2` |
| 3 | `published` | column | `slot_3` |
| 4 | `blah` | `attribute :blah` | `slot_4` |
| 5 | `extra` | `SELECT 1 AS extra` | by name |

So we have kind of namespaces where the beginning of the array is "columns from the database", the middle is "anything defined via custom attributes" and the end is "extra columns selected from the database".

title: Use an Array for storing Active Record attributes
